case_name: Clear Channel Outdoor, LLC v. Director of Finance, Baltimore City
title: Clear Channel Outdoor, LLC v. Director of Finance, Baltimore City
text:
CLEAR CHANNEL OUTDOOR, LLC * IN THE
*
*
*
*
vs. * MARYLAND TAX COURT
*
*
*
DIRECTOR, DEPARTMENT OF *
FINANCE OF BALTIMORE CITY * 23-MI-BA-0076
*
**********************************************************************
MEMORANDUM AND ORDER
Petitioner Clear Channel Outdoor, LLC (“Petitioner” or “Clear Channel”) has appealed a
decision by Respondent Department of Finance for Baltimore City (“Respondent” or “City”) to
deny the refund claims filed by Clear Channel for refunds of the Outdoor Advertising Tax, Title
28, Subtitle 29 of the Baltimore City Code (“Tax”) paid for in fiscal years 2019, 2020, and 2021.
In its petition of appeal, Clear Channel cites four independent issues paraphrased below:
1) There was no “use” by the advertisers under the Tax so Clear Channel was not an
“Advertising Host” as defined under the Tax and was not required to remit it.
2) The Tax is void for vagueness.
3) The Tax imposes an impermissible non-uniform property tax.
4) The Tax violates the equal protection clauses of the U.S. and Maryland Constitutions.
At the hearing, Clear Channel did not pursue issues 2 and 4. Nonetheless, Clear Channel
argued issue 2 in its post-hearing brief and so the Court provided a decision on issues 1 through
3.1 Both the petitioner and respondent submitted pre- and post-hearing briefs, which were
reviewed in detail.
The Tax Court’s jurisdiction is invoked under the Local Government article of the
Maryland Code, section § 20-117 as Clear Channel’s refund claimed was determined and
1 The Court notes that it would have analyzed issue 4 under the rationally related test.
1

investigated by the City under § 20-116 and Clear Channel was given notice under paragraph
(c)(1) of that subtitle on December 29, 2022.
For the reasons discussed below, the City’s decision to deny Clear Channel’s refund claim
of the Tax was proper. All claims by Clear Channel are hereby denied.
FACTUAL BACKGROUND2
While a Joint Stipulation of Facts was provided to the Court, along with several other
exhibits attached to the parties’ respective briefings, evidence and testimony from Michael Lund,
a Partner at Deloitte & Touche LLP, who served as an expert witness for accounting purposes,
and Daryl Hall, Vice President of Tax, who served as the corporate designee of the petitioner,
was provided to the Court at the hearing.
Clear Channel owned and controlled at least 694 outdoor advertising displays as defined
under the Tax in fiscal years 2019, 2020, and 2021 (together the “Fiscal Years at Issue”).3, 4 Stip.
at ¶¶ 10–12. Included in the advertising displays it owned and operated were non-electronic
static outdoor displays that had to be manually changed and electronic digital displays that could
change images more than once per day and could serve multiple customers of Clear Channel
(collectively called the “Billboards”). Id.
Clear Channel’s agreements with the City-as-customer generally provided that “[t]he
provision of advertising services by Clear Channel to Customer does not transfer any ownership
rights of any advertising structure. Customer acknowledges and agrees that no lease or license
shall arise from the provision of advertising services.” Stip. at ¶¶ 13 a–d, referencing Stipulation
Ex. D. at § 4.6, E. at § 4.6, F. at § 4.7, and G. at § 4.7.5 Clear Channel’s City customers did not
intend to lease or license the Billboards or use or possess the Billboards. Id. Clear Channel
owned and controlled the Billboards over the Fiscal Years at Issue. Stip. ¶ 15. Payments made
2 Citations to the Joint Stipulation of Facts provided by the parties before the hearing will be designated as “Stip. at
¶__” to mimic Clear Channel’s designation in its pre-hearing brief.
3 Specifically, as defined under § 29-1(d).
4 The Fiscal Years at Issue relate to the tax years ending on June 30, 2020 (calendar dates of July 1, 2019, through
June 30, 2020, “Fiscal Year 2019”), June 30, 2021 (calendar dates July 1, 2020, through June 30, 2021, “Fiscal Year
2020”), and June 30, 2022 (calendar dates of July 1, 2021, through June 30, 2022, “Fiscal Year 2021”).
5 Notably, no contracts between Clear Channel and its non-City customers were provided in the Joint Statement of
Facts. Those contracts were, however, provided through the City’s discovery requests.
2

by customers to Clear Channel related to the Billboards were recorded for financial statement
purposes as advertising expenses and not rent. Pet’r’s Hearing Ex. 1.
APPLICABLE LAW6
The Tax defines the key terms in contention. Paragraph b of the Tax defines “advertising
host” as “a person who: (1) owns or controls a billboard, posterboard, or other sign; and (2)
charges fees for its use as an outdoor advertising display.”7 Paragraph d of the Tax defines
“outdoor advertising display” as “an outdoor display of a 10 square foot or larger image or
message that directs attention to a business, commodity, service, event, or other activity that is:
(i) sold, offered, or conducted somewhere other than on the premises on which the display is
made; and (ii) sold, offered, or conducted on the premises only incidentally if at all.”8 A related
section of the Tax defines the required report that advertising hosts must file.9
ARGUMENT
As stated above, the Tax Court has proper jurisdiction to hear this appeal.10 As is the case
with Maryland’s state and local tax administrative processes, the determination “from which the
appeal is taken,” made by the City, is deemed prima facie correct.11 The burden of proof is on
Clear Channel to prove that the City’s denial was incorrect. Clear Channel failed to meet that
burden.
1) Clear Channel’s argument that ownership or control of the Billboards by advertisers is
required under the Tax is not persuasive.
Clear Channel contends that the advertisers, its customers, did not engage in any “use” under
the Tax. This means that Clear Channel does not qualify as an “Advertising Host.”
Consequently, Clear Channel was not obligated to pay the Tax. Clear Channel argues the Tax
6 Clear Channel presented the state statute MD. CODE ANN., TAX-GEN § 11-101(n)(1), which defines “use.” That
definition not only is defined by the Maryland General Assembly and not the City Council, but it provides that
definition for a different tax type. Notably, neither party argues that the Tax is a use tax, and the Court agrees that
the Tax is not a use tax.
7 § 29-1(b).
8 § 29-1(d).
9 § 29-5 (a)
10 Supra p. 2.
11 MD. CODE ANN., TAX-GEN. § 13-528(b).
3

applies solely to “advertising hosts,” whomever those people may be. Clear Channel’s argument
is flawed generally, but specifically, given the facts presented.
a) Its use refers to the use of the “billboard, posterboard, or other sign,” not for a particular
party’s use of the billboard.
The tax code definition of an “advertising host” means a person who: (1) owns or
controls a billboard, posterboard, or other sign; and (2) charges fees for its use as an outdoor
advertising display.12
Here, “its use” in plain language means the use of the “billboard, posterboard, or other
sign” for advertising. The Billboards that Clear Channel owned or controlled were used as
outdoor advertising displays according to Clear Channel’s testimony and briefs. Clear
Channel placed the advertisement on the Billboards and was responsible for maintaining the
billboards. Cherry v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore City, 475 Md. 565, 598 (2021)
(“The plain language of the local ordinance is the primary source of legislative intent.”). It is
clear that § 29-1(b) uses the possessive pronoun “its” in the phrase “charges fees for its use. .
. .” to refer to the preceding noun series, “a billboard, posterboard, or other sign.” There is
no other phrase under the Tax to which it could logically refer. Nowhere else in section § 29
is any language that even refers to an end-user advertiser. As such, it is not logical that “its
use” would refer to a party that was not even mentioned in the code.
An “advertising host” is a “person,” which includes Clear Channel.13 Here, Clear
Channel “owns or controls a billboard.” Id. at (b)(1).
b) Clear Channel’s argument that the term “use” in § 29-1(b) requires transfer of ownership
or control of the Billboards does not comport with the statute.
Clear Channel argues that it is not an “advertising host” because the advertisers that pay
Clear Channel to post their advertisements do not “use” the Billboards because the
advertisers do not own, maintain, or control the Billboards. Instead, Clear Channel erects the
signs and maintains the Billboards. The Billboards were clearly used as an outdoor
12 § 29-1(b) (emphasis added).
13 “ ‘Person’ means: (i) an individual; (ii) a partnership, firm, association, corporation, or other entity of any kind;
and (iii) a receiver, trustee, guardian, personal representative, fiduciary, or representative of any kind.” Id. at (e).
4

advertising display, so the Tax applies to Clear Channel. The code does not differentiate who
uses the Billboards. Where a word is used in a statute and not specifically defined, it should
be construed as having its ordinary and commonly accepted meaning. Wheeler v. State, 281
Md. 593, 596-97 (1977), cert. denied, 435 U.S. 997 (1978); Allen v. Mutual Fire Ins. Co., 2
Md. 111, 120-21 (1852); Quotron Systems v. Comptroller, 287 Md. 178, 187 n.5 (Md. 1980).
Further, there is nothing in the legislative history or in the statute that would lead anyone
to think that Clear Channel’s “use” of the Billboards would limit the tax applicability based
on whether an end-user advertiser had ownership and control of the Billboards. Clear
Channel argues that because the advertiser does not maintain, own, and cannot
physically/electronically put the actual advertisement on the billboard itself, the advertiser
cannot “use” the Billboards. The advertiser, however, does choose which advertisements,
including the layout, design, and text that is placed on the Billboards. Clear Channel’s
argument that, “the advertisers do nothing with the billboards,” is bold. The advertisers
control the main purpose of the Billboards‒the content that is placed on them.14
In its brief, Clear Channel argues that “most definitions [of use] contain a common
element–the user must be ‘doing something with’ an ‘object, machine, person, method, etc.’
in order to accomplish as task.” Pet’r’s Post-Hearing Brief at 11. Here, the advertisers that
pay Clear Channel a fee give Clear Channel the design, layout, and text‒ all essential parts of
the Billboards‒to place on the Billboard. In § 29-1(b), the word “use,” by its plain language
means to display something on a billboard, posterboard, or other sign. This interpretation is
also supported by an earlier Court of Appeals that addressed the same statute regarding Clear
Channel and the Tax. Clear Channel Outdoor, Inc. v. Dir., Dep't of Fin. of Balt. City, 472
Md. 444, 475 (Md. 2021) (“What matters is whether Clear Channel charges the person or
entity responsible for the message to display it on the billboard. . . . It is the commercial
transaction, not the content of the message, that triggers the tax.”).
Clear Channel also argues that the term “use” under the Maryland state-level sales and
use tax scheme might apply. That definition of “use” is “an exercise of a right or power to
use, consume, possess, or store: (1) tangible property; (ii) a taxable service; (iii) a digital
14 Even if Clear Channel structures its contracts with customers to maintain “exclusive possession and control,”
these contracts are not a vehicle to remove Clear Channel’s tax liabilities.
5

code; or (iv) a digital product.15 The state statute definition of “use” is not relevant as it was
not enacted by the Baltimore City Council, and it is described under a completely different
tax type. Also, the advertisers pay Clear Channel to place specified advertisements on the
Billboards for a fee, and in doing so, the advertisers are exercising some right over the use of
the Billboards even though the maintenance and ownership rights continue to be with Clear
Channel. Clear Channel cannot claim both that the advertisers do not “use” the Billboards
and that they also have control of the Billboards’ essential messaging.
Ultimately, there is no evidence that the City Council intended to apply the term “use”
from the Maryland Tax General statute. Clear Channel eschews the natural and ordinary
meaning of the word “use” in the Tax to apply an inapplicable meaning from a state statute.
Clear Channel’s interpretation does not conform to the plain language of the City code. Clear
Channel’s interpretation would render the provision meaningless.
c) Clear Channel’s reliance on Quotron is not persuasive.
Clear Channel cites Quotron to show that a taxable use requires a transfer of possession
of the property. The correct citation that Clear Channel did not fully represent is reproduced
below.
[This Court] determined, therefore, that [Chesapeake & Potomac Telephone Co.]
provided a service and not a mere rental of equipment, and held that the charges
received from the rendition of such communication services were not taxable
because of an exemption expressed in Art. 81, § 326(n).
Quotron Systems v. Comptroller, 287 Md. 178, 184 (Md. 1980) (citing the reasoning
for the Court’s decision in Comptroller of the Treasury v. Chesapeake & Potomac
Telephone Co., 241 Md. 345 (1966)) (emphasis added).
In Quotron, the Court of Appeals found that there were no taxable charges from the
“rendition of . . . . [c]ommunication services” provided by the hardware used in providing a
subscription for financial services. This decision depended on the exemption for taxation for
“transportation and communication services,” which is not applicable here. Id. Further, that
decision found “the hardware” that was not subject to a use tax “had no utility in and of itself
15 MD. CODE ANN., TAX-GEN. § 11-101(n)(1).
6

to Maryland subscribers.” Id. at 187. In this appeal, however, the Billboards (e.g. “the
hardware”) are paramount to the advertising services.
Further, Clear Channel advertisers had control of arguably the most important part of the
Billboards, those being the advertisements displayed. Also, unlike the code relevant to
Quotron, the Tax is an excise tax that is required when an advertising host uses the Billboard
as an outdoor advertising display. Further unlike in Quotron, where the service charges did
not reflect the value of the hardware, Clear Channel testified that the price Clear Channel
charged for the advertising services had to do primarily with the desirability of the
corresponding Billboards’ locations. In Quotron, “the service provided by Quotron required
the use of hardware which had no utility in and of itself to Maryland subscribers.” Id. at 188.
Here, the Billboards were essential to the advertising services. Unlike in Quotron, where the
hardware was incidental to the contract and Quotron controlled the hardware, the ability to
display an advertiser’s message on the Billboards was the main value captured in the
contracts and the advertisers controlled what message Clear Channel put on the Billboards
when it paid Clear Channel for advertising services.
d) Clear Channels other arguments against “use” are not persuasive.
Clear Channel’s argument about other states’ determination of taxes on billboards is not
authoritative in this Court, and Clear Channel does not discuss how those laws regarding
excise tax on Billboards are the same or different as the Tax, even though Clear Channel had
witnesses and an opportunity to provide relevant testimony.
Clear Channel’s argument that digital advertising services on the Billboards are not the
“use” of the Billboard is not persuasive because the purpose of the service and the purpose of
the digital billboard is to display the specific advertisements that Clear Channel’s customers
pay to have displayed on specific billboards at specific times.
Clear Channel’s argument about Internal Revenue Service’s rulings regarding billboard
arrangements are not applicable because they are an analysis of federal law, not Baltimore
City’s law. Similarly, companies’ accounting procedures, even under Generally Accepted
Accounting Principles, for payments under Clear Channel’s advertising services contracts are
irrelevant to the legal Tax considerations.
7

Clear Channel’s argument that “tax imposition provisions are to be narrowly construed
against the government because the government can take no more than has been clearly
authorized by the legislature” is also not persuasive because there is no ambiguity. Pet’r’s
Post-Hearing Br. At 14. The Court considered all testimony Clear Channel provided during
the hearing, all affidavits, and all briefs in making this determination.
e) Clear Channel is estopped from denying it is an “Advertising Host” under judicial
estoppel.
Clear Channel is precluded from denying that it is an “advertising host” under the Tax,
having taken a contrary position in previous litigation when it sought a refund of Tax for
other fiscal years. The prior litigation was focused on constitutional issues of the Tax, but in
order to have standing in the prior appeal, Clear Channel had to take the position, and indeed
did, that is was an “advertising host.”
Estoppel may be applied where three circumstances exist: “(1) one of the parties takes a
[] position that is, inconsistent with a position it took in previous litigation, (2) the previous
inconsistent position was accepted by a court, and (3) the party who is maintaining the
inconsistent positions must have intentionally misled the court in order to gain an unfair
advantage.” Haw v. Nat'l Collegiate Athletic Ass'n, 260 Md. App. 310, 365 (Md. Ct. Spec.
App. 2024) (internal citations omitted).
In previous litigation, Clear Channel challenged this “tax related to the sale of advertising
on its billboards . . . under the constitutional provisions that protect freedom of speech and of
the press.” Clear Channel Outdoor, Inc. v. Dir., Dep’t of Fin. of Baltimore City, 472 Md. 444,
450 (2021). For standing to raise this claim, Clear Channel took the position that the Tax
imposed a pecuniary burden on “all operators of off-site billboards in the City who sell
advertising on those billboards.” Id. at 472. Clear Channel argued that this increased tax
burden, as applied to Clear Channel, interfered “with First Amendment activities.” Id. The
fact that the tax years were different in this suit is not enough to allow Clear Channel to
relitigate the same issue. State Tax Comm’n of Md. v. Bullis Sch., Inc.,, 218 Md. 558, 563
(1959) (“different taxable years . . . is not controlling.”).
8

Importantly, the Court of Appeals of Maryland found, “[t]he [Tax] applies to all off-site
billboards in the City for which the operator charges customers for displaying the customer’s
advertising. It does not distinguish among billboards according to any other factor. . . .”
Clear Channel, 472 Md. at 474. As such, the factual information Clear Channel provided in
this appeal regarding how the Billboards are taxed for federal income taxes and its
customers’ lack of control of the Billboards beyond the messages placed on them would not
impact that decision. This is because that decision is defined when the statute applied in
clear language. Also, there was no compelling evidence that there were any changes in fact
or law that would modify the prior decision. This Court’s findings of fact and conclusions of
law compel it to find that estoppel is implicated.
All of the courts accepted Clear Channel’s position acknowledging tax liability as an
“advertising host” in the previous litigation. In this current proceeding, Clear Channel’s
denial of tax liability, and specifically its position as an “advertising host,” is inconsistent
with the accepted previous position. The causes of action in that appeal may not have been
all of the same issues raised in this one, but estoppel does not implicate all of Clear Channel’s
current claims. The same issue regarding “advertising host,” however, cannot be
inconsistent.
Further, the factual issues raised in this appeal did not help explain Clear Channel’s
inconsistent approach between the appeals.16 As such, Clear Channel is estopped from
arguing it is not an “advertising host” in this appeal.
2) The Tax is not void for vagueness.17
Clear Channel’s argument that “tax imposition provisions are to be narrowly construed
against the government because the government can take no more than has been clearly
authorized by the legislature” is not persuasive because there is no ambiguity or vagueness.
Pet’r’s Post-Hearing Br. at 14. The statute is clear on its face, as its use refers to the use of the
Billboard as an outdoor advertising display, not for a particular party’s use of the Billboard given
16 Clear Channel argued that the prior litigation was for other tax years. All of the relevant underlying law, and
nearly all of the facts other than the tax years appeared to have remained the same.
17 At the hearing, Clear Channel did not argue that the Tax is void for vagueness under procedural due process.
Clear Channel added the argument again in its post-hearing brief, though. The Court has addressed Clear Channel’s
argument as it was stated in the pre- and post-hearing briefs.
9

that no mention of the party owning the Billboard or paying for the advertising services is
mentioned elsewhere in the definition of “advertising host” in the Tax. The statute does not
differentiate between those who are using the Billboard. There is no textual or rational support
in the Tax or elsewhere to support that the Tax only applies if the end advertising customers have
rights to use or possess the Billboards. When an advertisement is placed on a billboard, the
billboard is being used as an advertising display.
3) The Tax does not impose an impermissible non-uniform property tax.
Clear Channel argues that under Weaver v. Prince George’s County, the Tax is actually a
property tax, not an excise tax.18 The Weaver Court looked at the following factors to determine
if a tax was an excise versus a property tax:
To draw that line here, we examine [1] the designation placed upon the tax by the
Legislature, [2] the subject matter of the tax, and [3] the incidents of the tax, i.e., the
manner in which it is assessed and the measure of the tax.
Weaver, 281 Md. 349 at 356.
Each Weaver factor is analyzed in turn.
a) First Factor: the designation placed upon the tax by the legislature supports that the
Billboard Tax is an excise tax because it is named as such in the code although it is not
determinative.
Baltimore City Code Art. 28 § 29-2 states, “An excise tax is imposed on the privilege of
exhibiting outdoor advertising displays in the City.” (emphasis added). Therefore, the City
designated the tax at issue as an excise tax.
b) Second Factor: the subject matter of the Tax relates to the use of billboards as outdoor
advertising displays, which does not support the Tax being classified as a property tax.
In analyzing the second prong of Weaver, that Court provided the guidance below.
In Continental Motors Corp. v. Township of Muskegon, 376 Mich. 170, 135
N.W.2d 908, 911 (1965), an excise was defined as ‘a tax imposed upon the
performance of an act, the engaging in an occupation, or the enjoyment of a
18 Weaver v. Prince George's County, 281 Md. 349 (1977).
10

privilege.’ Indeed, an excise is said to embrace every form of taxation that is not
a burden directly imposed on persons or property.
Weaver, 281 Md. 349 at 357–58 (internal citations and emphasis removed).
Here, the subject matter of the tax is outdoor advertising. The Tax is “not a burden
directly imposed on persons or property,” as no tax would be required if a billboard is blank.
After all, under the Tax, only those signs that contain advertisements are taxed. Further,
advertising a large display is “the performance of an act. . . or the enjoyment of a privilege,"
so the subject matter of the tax supports the classification of an excise tax. Id.
Clear Channel argues that the Billboard has “only one possible operation or purpose–to
post advertising message.” Pet’r’s Post-Hearing Br. at 7. The Weaver Court explained: “The
privilege of using property is only one of the many incidents which make up the bundle of
rights, powers, privileges and immunities, collectively regarded as property or ownership.”
Id. at 359. “As the Supreme Court stated in Bromley v. McCaughn, 280 U.S. at 136, ‘a tax
imposed upon a particular use of property or the exercise of a single power incident to
ownership, is an excise.’ ” Id. The only subject matter in this appeal is the displaying of
advertising on Billboards.
c) Third Factor: the manner in which the Tax is assessed does not support a finding that the
Tax operates as a property tax.
The Weaver Court stated:
[I]t has been held that where a tax is levied directly by the Legislature
without assessment and is measured by the extent to which a privilege is
exercised by a taxpayer without regard to the nature or value of his assets,
it is an excise. Where, however, the tax is computed upon a valuation of the
property and is assessed by assessors, and where the failure to pay the tax
results in a lien against the property, it is a property tax, even though a
privilege might be included in the valuation.
Id. at 358 (internal citations omitted).19
The Tax is not based on the assessment of the property value of the outdoor
advertisement or any other such valuation of property. The Tax does not take into account
19 This Court notes that this is another instance when Clear Channel did not fully represent full quotations of case
law.
11

the location of the Billboard, but instead is based on its size and type. There are no assessors
involved as the advertising host must self-report the amount of Tax to be paid. Therefore,
this third factor supports the Tax to be an excise tax.
Lastly on this issue, the Maryland Tax Court, the Maryland Court of Special Appeals, and
the Maryland Court of Appeals consistently stated that this “[o]rdinance is a valid excise
tax.” See for example Clear Channel Outdoor, Inc. v. Dir., Dep't. of Fin. of Balt. City, 244
Md. App. 304, 313 (Md. Ct. Spec. App. 2020).
d) Clear Channel’s argument that the Tax is non-uniform is not persuasive.
Clear Channel argues that the Tax is non-uniform within the same class within the state.
First, Clear Channel points out that advertising space on billboards that is smaller than 10
square feet is not subject to the Tax no matter how large the Billboard. Article 15 of the
Maryland Declaration of Rights states that taxes “shall be uniform within each class or sub-
class of land, improvements on land and personal property which the respective taxing
powers may have directed to be subjected to the tax levy.” The Tax is uniform, as all
billboards that have advertisements less than 10 square feet are not taxed. Clear Channel,
like all other similarly situated individuals, could decide to reduce the advertising space on
its billboards to not be subject to the Tax.
Clear Channel also argues electronic billboards are taxed at a higher rate than static
billboards, so the tax is non-uniform. Electronic and static billboards are two different
subclasses of billboards. Electronic billboards, after all, can change advertisements multiple
times a day without manual effort, can include visual effects to make them more noticeable,
and require a different level of technology than static billboards. Further, the displays on
electronic and on static billboards are different, which are reflected in the price difference of
the two billboard subclasses in the same location. Therefore, the tax is uniform.
Lastly, the Tax is not subject to constitutional uniformity. Oursler v. Tawes, 178 Md. 471,
486 (Md. 1940) (“Legislature may levy, not upon property, but upon occupations, privileges,
contracts and things of that nature, and as to those the rule of equality is not applicable.”).
12
